[MUQATIL:7:19-21/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Muqatil identifies the forbidden tree as a wheat stalk.
[MUQATIL:7:19-21/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | reports | He also reports an unnamed view that it was the tree beneath which angels rub themselves to gain immortality.
[MUQATIL:7:19-21/r3] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Eating from the tree would make Adam and his wife wrong themselves.
[TAB-FULL:v10p106/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | After expelling Iblis from the Garden, God settled Adam and his wife there, allowed them to eat fruit wherever they wished, and forbade them to approach one particular tree.
[TAB-FULL:v10p106/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Being among the wrongdoers means opposing the Lord’s command and doing what one has no right to do; Tabari gives the same gloss at 2:35. | mentions 2:35
[ZAJJAJ:v2p325/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | prefers | Including the independent pronoun أنت is the better construction; اذهب وزيد without it would be awkward.
[ZAJJAJ:v2p326/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · بعضهم | reports | Some identify the forbidden tree as wheat; another view identifies it as a grapevine.
[ZAJJAJ:v2p326/r2] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | prefers | The preferred parse makes فتكونا accusative as the consequence of the prohibition: if they approach, they become wrongdoers.
[ZAJJAJ:v2p326/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | Alternatively فتكونا is jussive, coordinated with the prohibition: do not approach, and so do not become wrongdoers.
[IBNABIHATIM:v5p1448/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · أبو العالية | reports | Abū al-ʿĀliya reports that God created Adam on Friday and placed him in the Garden of Firdaws that same day.
[IBNABIHATIM:v5p1448/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddī recounts that Adam first lived alone in the Garden, then awoke to a woman made from his rib to be his companion; she was named Ḥawwāʾ because she came from something living.
[IBNABIHATIM:v5p1448/r3] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · أشعث الحداني | reports | Ashʿath al-Ḥaddānī says Ḥawwāʾ was one of the women of the Garden, and her pregnancy was so clear that the child’s sex could be seen.
[IBNABIHATIM:v5p1448/r4] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid says Adam and his wife could eat wherever they wished without being held to account.
[IBNABIHATIM:v5p1448/r5] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the forbidden tree as a grapevine; Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, al-Shaʿbī, Jaʿd ibn Hubayra, al-Suddī, and Muḥammad ibn Qays agree.
[IBNABIHATIM:v5p1449/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda says God tested Adam as He had tested the angels before; all creation is tested for obedience, and Adam's trial continued until he violated the prohibition.
[IBNABIHATIM:v5p1449/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · وهب بن منبه | reports | Wahb ibn Munabbih says the tree was barley; each grain in the Garden was as large as a cow's liver, softer than butter, and sweeter than honey.
[IBNABIHATIM:v5p1449/r3] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · أبو مالك | reports | Abū Mālik identifies the forbidden tree as a date palm.
[IBNABIHATIM:v5p1449/r4] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda identifies the forbidden tree as a fig; Mujāhid and Ibn Jurayj report the same view.
[IBNABIHATIM:v5p1449/r5] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · أبو العالية | reports | Abū al-ʿĀliya says eating from the tree caused bodily evacuation, which would be improper in the Garden.
[IBNABIHATIM:v5p1449/r6] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · وهب بن منبه | reports | Wahb says the tree had intertwined, branching limbs and bore fruit eaten by angels for immortality; this was the fruit forbidden to Adam and his wife.
[NAHHAS:v2p117/r9] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | The command is a prohibition, and ‘then you will be among the wrongdoers’ is its coordinated consequence.
[SULAMI:v1p223#3/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · قيل | reports | One account says Adam understood the prohibition to concern the particular tree indicated, while God intended its whole kind; he took another, and repented for failing to be cautious rather than for disobedience.
[SULAMI:v1p223#3/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · الخراز | reports | Al-Kharr az says the command and prohibition made Adam uneasy even in Paradise; God let the lapse occur so its lesson and proof would emerge, then expelled and reproached him, with 20:115 also cited. | mentions 20:115
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p208#2/r1] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Adam's wife is Eve (Hawwa).
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p208#2/r10] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · محمد بن إسحاق | rejects | Ibn Ishaq transmits from the People of the Two Books that it was a colocynth tree, but al-Mawardi says he knows no basis for this report.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p208#2/r11] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | The prohibition despite their complete knowledge served to preserve that knowledge and test them in a matter for which they would receive recompense.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p208#2/r2] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | The garden may be the promised Garden of Eternity, from which departure was possible because it was not a reward requiring permanent residence, or an earthly garden without duties, although Adam himself was obligated.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p208#2/r3] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | Permission may cover any place throughout the garden, or any of its fruits, since the forbidden tree was fruit-bearing.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p208#2/r4] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas identifies the forbidden tree as wheat.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p208#2/r5] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddi identifies the forbidden tree as a grapevine.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p208#2/r6] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · بان جريج | reports | Ibn Jurayj identifies the forbidden tree as a fig tree.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p208#2/r7] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · علي بن أبي طالب | reports | Ali ibn Abi Talib identifies it as a camphor tree.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p208#2/r8] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · الكلبي | reports | Al-Kalbi identifies it as the tree of knowledge.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p208#2/r9] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · ابن جدعان | reports | Ibn Jud'an identifies it as the tree of eternity, which the angels ate from.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p325/r10] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | God placed the means of trial with Adam in the Garden: his spouse and the tree of ordeal; the tree’s presence reflects the hidden mystery of divine allotment.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p60/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The explanation of this verse is given in Surat al-Baqara. | mentions 2:35
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:7:19-22/r1] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | The author says the explanation of Adam being told to dwell in the Garden was already given in al-Baqara. | mentions 2, :, 3, 5
[DAMGHANI:v1p34/r2] DAMGHANI, d. 478 · author | holds | Al-akl can mean eating itself; Ṭā Hā is a parallel. | mentions 20:121
[DAMGHANI:v1p420/r26] DAMGHANI, d. 478 · author | holds | Lā can mark prohibition, as in the ban on approaching the tree or consuming one another's property unjustly.
[JISHUMI:v4p2520/r10] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Not approaching the tree means avoiding it.
[JISHUMI:v4p2520/r11] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الأكثر | reports | Most hold that the prohibition was binding and legally prohibitive; another view treats it as a nonbinding discouragement.
[JISHUMI:v4p2520/r12] JISHUMI, d. 494 · قيل | reports | One reported identification of the forbidden tree is the grapevine.
[JISHUMI:v4p2520/r13] JISHUMI, d. 494 · قيل | reports | Another reported identification of the forbidden tree is wheat.
[JISHUMI:v4p2520/r14] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The word tree can denote anything with a trunk.
[JISHUMI:v4p2520/r15] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | They would wrong themselves by eating from it; the wording is a threat.
[JISHUMI:v4p2520/r16] JISHUMI, d. 494 · قيل | reports | One explanation of their lapse is that they forgot the threat and thought the prohibition was only discouraging.
[JISHUMI:v4p2520/r17] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو علي | prefers | Abu Ali explains that they misread the prohibition as applying to one particular tree, then ate from the same kind; the author calls this the soundest view.
[JISHUMI:v4p2520/r18] JISHUMI, d. 494 · قيل | reports | A third explanation is that they forgot the prohibition; the author says a prohibition is not binding when forgotten, supporting Abu Ali’s view.
[JISHUMI:v4p2520/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Adam’s wife is Eve; the masculine wording is used because the possessive relation to Adam conveys the intended meaning concisely.
[JISHUMI:v4p2520/r5] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو علي وأبو هاشم | reports | One view identifies this garden as a garden among the gardens of heaven.
[JISHUMI:v4p2520/r6] JISHUMI, d. 494 · علي بن عيسى | reports | A group identifies the garden as the Garden of Eternity; this is the choice of Ali ibn Isa.
[JISHUMI:v4p2520/r7] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The story is repeated because the Quran descended over twenty-odd years amid changing circumstances and visiting delegations, so new listeners could hear it as instruction and kindness.
[JISHUMI:v4p2520/r8] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Repeating one story in different, excellent formulations is one aspect of the Quran’s inimitability.
[JISHUMI:v4p2520/r9] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The command to eat grants permission to enjoy the garden’s blessings wherever they wish.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p90#3/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The address يا آدم is explained as God saying to Adam, ‘O Adam.’
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p382#2/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The final ha in هذه is a ya changed at pause and retained in connected speech; Ibn Muhaysin's هذي preserves the original form.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p382#2/r10] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · بعضهم | reports | One rationalist view holds everything prohibited until permission arrives, since using another's property is an encroachment, especially in relation to God.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p382#2/r11] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · بعض هذه الفرقة | reports | Some in that group exempt breathing and mo

vement because they cannot do otherwise.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p382#2/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · ابن محيصن | reports | Ibn Muhaysin reads هذي الشجرة, preserving the original form.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p382#2/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | فتكونا is subjunctive as the response to the prohibition.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p382#2/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Jurists discuss how to judge unprecedented cases without a specific Qur'anic, Prophetic, or consensus ruling, then consider analogy and the default status of acts.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p382#2/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · بعضهم | reports | One juristic view defaults to prohibition and caution: omission of a new case does not authorize people to legislate its permissibility.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p382#2/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · بعضهم | reports | Another juristic view defaults to permissibility until a prohibition appears, since God completed the religion and would not leave people ignorant of an intended ban.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p382#2/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · بعضهم | prefers | A third juristic view suspends judgment and continues inquiry because cases require a specific or general revealed ruling; Ibn Atiyya calls this clearest.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p382#2/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The jurists' debate concerns deriving rulings from revelation, not whether reason independently makes actions good or bad.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p382#2/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · المعتزلة ومن قال بقولهم | reports | The Muʿtazila frame the issue through rational good and evil, imagining a time or person without revelation, or Adam before earthly commands.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p382/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | A command to do what someone already does tells them to continue and persist in that state.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p382/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | أنت emphasizes the hidden subject of اسكن and permits coordination with زوجك; the hidden pronoun especially needs emphasis.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p382/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | فكلا derives from أكل; its initial radical is omitted in this imperative pattern, partly to avoid a difficult vowel on a weak letter.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p382/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The verb is also used as قرب يقرب.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p382/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | reports | The demonstrative may indicate one tree of a kind, or one individual while meaning the whole kind, as in generic singulars.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p382/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Most exegetes say Adam knowingly intended the forbidden act; Iblis claimed the ban was meant to prevent immortality or angelhood.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p382/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | rejects | Ibn Atiyya rejects the claim that Adam mistook the ban as applying to one tree and ate another: this cannot explain why Iblis's promise persuaded him to violate what he thought allowed.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p383/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Ibn Atiyya says necessity could make breathing and movement permissible.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p383/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · بعضهم | reports | Another rationalist view allows harmless use of another's property, such as shade by a wall, and argues this is all the more permissible with God, who suffers no harm.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p383/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · أهل الحق والسنة | holds | The people of truth and Sunna say reason alone establishes neither binding good nor bad; such judgments arise only through revelation.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p383/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · بعضهم | reports | Some say reason is never without revelation, making the hypothetical meaningless; Adam received commands in Paradise, including praise after sneezing and instructions to dwell, eat, and avoid the tree.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p383/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · القاضي ابن الباقلاني | reports | In al-Taqrib wa-l-Irshad, Ibn al-Baqillani says jurists adopted the Muʿtazili argument without realizing its implications.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p383/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | rejects | Ibn Atiyya objects that this disparages jurists: they derived rulings for new cases from revelation and should not be accused of rejecting this theological principle.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p383/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Ibn Atiyya points back to his earlier discussion in al-Baqara about which tree it was.
[TABRISI:7:18-20/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The prohibition against approaching the tree means they must not eat from it.
[TABRISI:7:18-20/r11] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | They would wrong themselves by forfeiting the great reward.
[TABRISI:7:18-20/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The command is to dwell in the Garden, not merely to be still; zawjatuka is omitted because the possessive phrase already conveys its meaning concisely.
[TABRISI:7:18-20/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | God permits the two to eat from wherever they wish, in whatever place or manner they choose.
[RAZI-FULL:v14p37#3/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Razi lists ten issues deferred to al-Baqara: whether dwelling is worship or permission, Eve’s creation, the garden’s location, eating as permission, prohibition as disapproval or ban, tree identity and kind, sin severity, injustice and condemnation, and whether this preceded Adam’s prophethood. | mentions 2:35, 11:18
[RAZI-FULL:v14p37#3/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The remaining difference from 2:35 is waw there versus fa here: waw gives conjunction generally, while fa adds succession, so succession is a subtype of conjunction. | mentions 2:35
[RAZI-FULL:v14p37#3/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi resolves the wording difference by saying al-Baqara gives the general category, while al-Aʿraf specifies the particular kind of conjunction. | mentions 2:35
[QURTUBI-FULL:7:19/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | After Iblis was expelled from his place in heaven, Adam and Eve were told to dwell in the Garden; al-Qurtubi refers to his discussion of dwelling and the tree in al-Baqara. | mentions 2:35
[BAYDAWI-FULL:7:18-19/r6] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The implied wording is “And We said: O Adam.”
[BAYDAWI-FULL:7:18-19/r7] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | The variant hādhī is described as original from the diminutive dhayyā, with hāʾ substituted for yāʾ.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:7:18-19/r8] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The warning means they would become people who wronged themselves.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:7:18-19/r9] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Takūnā may be jussive by coordination or subjunctive as the consequence of the prohibition.
[NASAFI-FULL:v2p6#2/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | God addressed Adam after expelling Iblīs from the Garden.
[NASAFI-FULL:v2p6#2/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | «Dwell» means take the Garden as your residence.
[NASAFI-FULL:v2p6#2/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | They could eat wherever they wished but were forbidden to approach the tree lest they become wrongdoers.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p24/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The command begins with an understood and We said; its explanation had already appeared in al-Baqara, where the food is called abundant, a phrase omitted here for brevity. | mentions 2:35
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p24/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The wording in al-Baqara is fuller because that sūra is Medinan, whereas this Meccan passage expresses the same meaning more briefly. | mentions 2:35
[SAMIN-DURR:7:19/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The word رغدا found in al-Baqara is omitted here, but context indicates it. | mentions 2:35
[BURHAN:v2p410/r7] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | A connected subject pronoun is conventionally reinforced by an independent pronoun when coordinated with a noun.
[BURHAN:v4p107/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · ابن عمرون وابن مالك | reports | Ibn ʿUmarūn and Ibn Mālik require coordinated nouns to be capable of the same syntactic role; they therefore analyze زوجك as a separate clause with an omitted command to dwell.
[BURHAN:v4p107/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · أبو حيان | rejects | Abū Ḥayyān rejects that restriction: feminine Hind and masculine Zayd can be coordinated in تقوم هند وزيد even though Zayd alone cannot be the feminine verb’s subject.
[BURHAN:v4p144/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | In “do not approach this tree lest you become wrongdoers,” the verb after ف may be jussive, extending the prohibition to becoming wrongdoers, or subjunctive, expressing the consequence.
[BURHAN:v4p145/r9] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The prohibition against approaching the tree, followed by its consequence, is cited as a parallel.
[BIQAI-FULL:v3p14/r10] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The phrase means ample provision and permits eating from everything in the Garden except the forbidden tree; al-Baqara additionally indicates freedom to eat anywhere there. | mentions 2:35
[BIQAI-FULL:v3p14/r11] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Prohibiting even approach is stronger than merely forbidding eating: one who comes near a forbidden boundary may fall into the act itself.
[BIQAI-FULL:v3p14/r12] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Eating after approaching the tree would make them wrongdoers, like people walking in darkness; the episode warns that disobeying God can destroy even the highest station.
[BIQAI-FULL:v3p14/r8] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The explicit أنت confirms that the command addresses Adam himself, not a metonymic substitute among those associated with him.
[BIQAI-FULL:v3p14/r9] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The fāʾ in 'then eat' indicates that eating accompanied settlement in the Garden; al-Baqara's conjunction with waw does not conflict, since a specific sequence is contained within a general one. | mentions 2:35
[ITQAN:v3p304/r4] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | reports | Baqara’s ‘and eat’ uses waw to join dwelling and e

ating, while al-A‘raf’s fa follows taking a dwelling; ‘freely’ and ‘wherever you wish’ there fit the broader wording. | mentions 2:35, 7:19
[ITQAN:v3p305/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | In comparing Adam’s garden instructions, al-Araf’s fa marks eating as following the commanded taking up of residence, while min ḥaythu is less general than ḥaythu shiʾtum.
[BURSEVI:v3p109#2/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | The passage cites a report that God forgives believers' mountain-sized sins and places them on Jews and Christians.
[BURSEVI:v3p109#2/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | He says it accords with divine favor toward believers to ransom them through unbelievers: justice toward sinners and grace toward the obedient, against Mu'tazila denial.
[BURSEVI:v3p109#2/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | rejects | The Mu'tazila cite 6:164, but 29:13 says unbelievers bear their own and additional burdens; each unbeliever is still punished for their own sin. | mentions 6:164, 29:13
[BURSEVI:v3p109#2/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | God addressed Adam after expelling Iblis from the Garden.
[BURSEVI:v3p109#2/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The command means reside in a way that permits their stay and honors them.
[BURSEVI:v3p109#2/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Adam's spouse is Eve.
[BURSEVI:v3p109#2/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | In Arabic زوج can mean the single counterpart in a pair; two companions are called زوجان.
[BURSEVI:v3p109#3/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · أكثر أهل العلم | reports | Most scholars hold this is the Garden of eternal recompense.
[BURSEVI:v3p109#3/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · بعض المحققين من أهل الظاهر والباطن | reports | Some careful outward and inward scholars say it was either a garden in heaven from which they descended or an earthly garden elevated above the surrounding land.
[BURSEVI:v3p109#3/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · بعض المحققين من أهل الظاهر والباطن | reports | They argue it was a test garden: the final Garden has no prohibition; Adam slept, was expelled, and Iblis entered, unlike the Garden of recompense.
[BURSEVI:v3p109#3/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | A report says Adam craved grapes from the Garden at death; his sons went to find them, but angels met them and tended to Adam's burial.
[BURSEVI:v3p109#3/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | prefers | He concludes Adam's garden was on earth: his sons sought its grapes, and the Nile is said to emerge from the Garden, which he identifies with earthly gardens.
[BURSEVI:v3p109#3/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The pair could eat wherever they wished and freely enjoy the Garden's fruits and blessings.
[BURSEVI:v3p110/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | God left the tree unidentified; if naming it benefited people, He would have specified it, as Akam al-Marjan says.
[BURSEVI:v3p110/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Becoming wrongdoers means wronging themselves.
[ALUSI-FULL:v8p98#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | prefers | The implied “We said” is understood from 2:35; many investigators connect this whole episode to the earlier command to the angels, as a continuation of favor to humanity and honor for Adam. | mentions 2:34, 2:35
[ALUSI-FULL:v8p98#2/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | “You become” can be jussive, coordinated with “approach,” or subjunctive as the consequence of the prohibition.
